The ***Architecture Diagram*** given above explains the high-level design of the App.
The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W14-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W14-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**

The *Sequence Diagram* below shows the general interaction between components when the user issues a command. In CampusContacts, a contact is addressed by its name and, when required, its displayed suffix (for example, `delete John Tan_2`).
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W14-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)
<puml src="diagrams/UiClassDiagram.puml" alt="Structure of the UI Component"/>

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, `StatusBarFooter`,  `HelpWindow`, and `ContactDetailsWindow`. All of these, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W14-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-W14-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.
* opens a `ContactDetailsWindow` when a successful `show` command returns a selected contact in its `CommandResult`.
Here's a (partial) class diagram of the `Logic` component:

The sequence diagram below illustrates the interactions within the `Logic` component. The current delete command identifies a contact by name and optional suffix, for example `execute("delete John Tan_2")`.
<puml src="diagrams/DeleteSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Interactions Inside the Logic Component for a delete command" />
**Note:** The lifeline for `DeleteCommandParser` should end at the destroy marker (X), but due to a limitation of PlantUML, the lifeline continues till the end of diagram.

1. When `Logic` is called upon to execute a command, the command is passed to an `AddressBookParser` object, which in turn creates a parser that matches the command (e.g., `DeleteCommandParser`) and uses it to parse the command.
1. This results in a `Command` object (more precisely, an object of one of its subclasses e.g., `DeleteCommand`) which is executed by the `LogicManager`.
1. The command can communicate with the `Model` when it is executed (e.g. to delete a person).
Note that although this is shown as a single step in the diagram above for simplicity, the code can require several interactions between the command object and the `Model` to complete the operation.
1. The result of the command execution is encapsulated as a `CommandResult` object which is returned from `Logic`.
Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.

* `AddCommandParser` recognises `/role`, `/email`, `/phone`, and `/location`, and uses the tokenizer's preamble as the name. It rejects missing fields and duplicate required prefixes, then delegates value validation to `ParserUtil`. Location maps to the existing `Address` value object. Optional tags retain `t/` (or `/tag`); `edit` and `find` use corresponding slash prefixes. Storage and duplicate-name suffix allocation remain model/storage responsibilities, not parser responsibilities.
* `ShowCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser` accept `NAME[_NUMBER]`. The optional number selects a particular contact from a name bucket; omitting it selects the unsuffixed contact.
* stores address book data in a `UniquePersonHashMap`. It groups contacts by their base name and stores each group in a `TreeMap<Integer, Person>`.

* [gives each stored contact a `PersonIndex`](#add-command-parsing). The first contact in a name bucket has index `0` and is displayed without a suffix; subsequent contacts are displayed with a suffix derived from their 1-based index, such as `John Tan_2`.
* keeps an unmodifiable flattened `ObservableList<Person>` ordered by base name and then bucket index. This preserves a straightforward list for the existing UI and filtered views.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)
* saves contacts as nested name buckets under `personsByName`. Each bucket stores a map from the zero-based `PersonIndex` to the contact data.
* supports legacy flat `persons` JSON files when loading. They are converted into buckets in memory and are saved in the new nested form on the next write.
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.

The CampusContacts development team has decided to allow duplicate names, and assign indices to them for identification. For clean storing & restoring these indices upon reload, and efficient reuse of free indices, our team takes the following two-step approach to adding a person:

1. When a new contact is added, the command first supplies the model with an immutable `UnindexedPerson`. This object carries the validated contact details but has no `PersonIndex`, so it is not stored directly.

2. `UniquePersonHashMap` finds the contact’s name bucket, allocates the smallest available zero-based index, and calls `UnindexedPerson#withPersonIndex(...)` to create the indexed `Person` that is inserted into the bucket.
The original `UnindexedPerson` is no longer referenced after this operation and becomes eligible for garbage collection; it is not explicitly destroyed by the program.

After insertion, the name bucket remains ordered by index, while the outer map keeps contacts grouped by base name. The flattened observable list is then rebuilt in name-and-index order so existing list and filtered views receive the updated data. This separation allows parsing and command execution to work with a temporary unindexed value while the model remains responsible for assigning storage identity.
Here's a visualization of adding a person in action:
<puml src="diagrams/AddSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Parsing and executing an add command" />

CampusContacts allows several contacts to share the same name. `AddressBook` owns a `UniquePersonHashMap`, whose outer `TreeMap` groups contacts by name. Each group is a `PersonNameBucket` containing:
* a `TreeMap<Integer, Person>` for deterministic ordering by `PersonIndex`;
* a priority queue of released indexes, so the smallest available index is reused after a deletion; and
* the next new index to use when there is no released index.

When an `UnindexedPerson` is added, `UniquePersonHashMap` allocates an index and creates the corresponding indexed `Person`. Removing a contact releases its index. The map then refreshes its flattened observable list so the existing list UI remains in sync.
The storage snapshot is structured as follows:

On startup, `JsonSerializableAddressBook` validates each bucket, recreates the indexed `Person` objects from the nested map keys, and passes the result to `AddressBook#setPersonBuckets`. The name bucket rebuilds its released-index queue and next-index value once. Normal add, delete, and edit operations use the in-memory map; `LogicManager` subsequently saves a snapshot through `Storage`.
### Exclusive access to the data folder
`MainApp` acquires a `DataFileLock` before reading contacts or initializing preferences (which also writes to disk).
The lock uses `FileChannel.tryLock()` on `data/campuscontacts.json.lock` and remains held until shutdown finishes
saving preferences. A second launch using the same folder shows an error and exits without initializing its model
or saving preferences. Locking errors also prevent startup; the application does not continue without protection.
The sidecar file stays on disk after exit. Ownership comes from the operating-system lock, not the file's existence,
so an unexpected process exit does not require deleting a stale file. Deleting or replacing the sidecar while the app
is running would undermine this protection. A small synchronized registry rejects repeat acquisitions in the same
JVM before opening another channel, since closing such a channel can release process-level locks on some systems.
This protects app instances using the same data folder; it does not prevent external editors or older app versions
that do not acquire this lock from changing the JSON file.

A contact may have an optional `Photo` reference. When a photo is supplied to `add`, `StorageManager` delegates copying it into the application's `photos` directory to `PhotoStorage`; the contact keeps the returned relative path. `JsonAdaptedPerson` writes that reference to JSON, so the application can resolve the copied photo after restarting. The diagram focuses on the photo-specific fields and storage API; unrelated address-book storage details are omitted.
<puml src="diagrams/PhotoStorageClassDiagram.puml" alt="Class diagram of contact photo references and photo storage" width="550" />

The `show NAME[_NUMBER]` command lets users view the complete stored details of a specific contact without changing its profile fields. A successful selection updates the recently viewed history and, when the recent list is active, moves that contact to the front of the displayed list.
1. `ShowCommand` looks for the matching name and `PersonIndex` in the address book.
1. On success, it returns a `CommandResult` containing the selected `Person`.
1. The popup displays the contact's display name, ID, role, phone number, email, location, role-specific academic details, tags, creation and edit timestamps, and photo.
The popup is deliberately a UI concern: the command resolves a model object. `LogicManager` records a successful
selection in the recently viewed history, saves the address book, then returns the result to the UI.
`AddressBook` stores up to ten recently viewed contact identifiers, newest first. Each identifier is the
contact's existing name and optional suffix. Reopening a contact moves it to the front. Opening an eleventh
distinct contact removes the oldest entry. Callers receive an immutable copy of the history.
<puml src="diagrams/RecentContactsSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Recording a profile selection and handling save errors" />
`ShowCommand` finds a contact in the address book and returns it in `CommandResult`.
`LogicManager` then records the visit and saves the address book. If saving throws `IOException`, including
a permission error, it restores the previous history and reports the error instead of opening the popup.
A failed contact lookup leaves history unchanged.
`RecentCommand` asks `ModelManager` to show contacts in history order using the existing `FilteredList`
and `SortedList`. This does not change the sort preference in `UserPrefs`. Reopening a contact refreshes
an active recent view. `list`, add or another filter restores the saved sort order. An explicit `sort`
orders the current results normally; `recent` returns them to history order.
A missing or null array loads as empty history. Loading removes missing contacts and repeated identifiers,
then keeps the first ten entries. Null entries or an invalid array structure cause a data-loading error.
Deleting a contact removes its history entry before the suffix can be reused. Editing a contact preserves
its position in history and keeps the recent view active; if its name changes, the history entry is updated
to the new display name. Replacing or clearing the address book also replaces the history.
An ordered list is enough for this feature: it avoids timestamps, tied visit times and changes to profile
constructors. Tests cover the ten-contact limit, repeat visits, duplicate names, filters, sorting, storage,
photos, deletion, clear confirmation and failed saves. Manual checks are listed below.
`SetFavouriteCommand` marks or unmarks a contact using the existing `NameIndexParser` grammar.
It searches the whole address book, so users can mark a contact even when it is hidden by a filter.
`ListFavouritesCommand` shows the selected contacts in the user's chosen sort order.
The status command checks the previous selection before updating it, so its feedback distinguishes
an added or removed favourite from an unchanged selection on repeated commands.
`AddressBook` stores favourites as a set of display identifiers: a name and its optional suffix.
These identifiers are unique because contact names cannot contain underscores. Storing selections
separately lets the feature work without changing `Person`, its subclasses or photo handling.
Callers receive an immutable snapshot of the set.
<puml src="diagrams/FavouritesSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Marking and listing a favourite contact" />
While the favourites view is active, `ModelManager` refreshes it after a status change or edit.
`list` and add return to the full contact list. `AddressBook#setPerson` keeps a contact's selection
when its identifier changes. Deleting or clearing contacts removes their selections, so a new
contact that reuses a suffix starts unmarked.
A missing or null array loads as an empty set. References to missing contacts are ignored;
an invalid array structure or null entry causes a data-loading error.
`LogicManager` saves the selections through the existing address-book save flow.
Tests cover identifier parsing, repeated commands, filtered views, sorting, JSON compatibility,
photo preservation, deletion, suffix reuse and clear confirmation. Manual checks are listed below.

The proposed undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedAddressBook`. It extends `AddressBook` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as an `addressBookStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedAddressBook#commit()` -- Saves the current address book state in its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#undo()` -- Restores the previous address book state from its history.
* `VersionedAddressBook#redo()` -- Restores a previously undone address book state from its history.
These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` and `Model#redoAddressBook()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedAddressBook` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single address book state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete John Tan_2` command to delete the second John Tan in the address book. The `delete` command calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing the modified state of the address book after the `delete John Tan_2` command executes to be saved in the `addressBookStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.

Step 3. The user executes `add David …​` to add a new person. The `add` command also calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.
**Note:** If a command fails its execution, it will not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, so the address book state will not be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which will shift the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state.

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial AddressBook state, then there are no previous AddressBook states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather
than attempting to perform the undo.
The following sequence diagram shows how an undo operation goes through the `Logic` component:
**Note:** The lifeline for `UndoCommand` should end at the destroy marker (X), but due to a limitation of PlantUML, it continues to the end of the diagram.
Similarly, how an undo operation goes through the `Model` component is shown below:

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `addressBookStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone AddressBook states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. Commands that do not modify the address book, such as `list`, will usually not call `Model#commitAddressBook()`, `Model#undoAddressBook()` or `Model#redoAddressBook()`. Thus, the `addressBookStateList` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear` and confirms with `yes`, which calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `addressBookStateList`, all address book states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add David …` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.
The following activity diagram summarizes what happens when a user executes a new command:
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Saves the entire address book.
* Cons: May have performance issues in terms of memory usage.
* **Alternative 2:** Individual command knows how to undo/redo by
* Pros: Will use less memory (e.g. for `delete`, just save the person being deleted).
* Cons: We must ensure that the implementation of each individual command is correct.

An archiving command will allow users to export inactive or past-semester contacts into an archive JSON file under `data/archive/` while removing them from the active `campuscontacts.json` to maintain responsiveness.
* is a university student or teaching staff member
* has a need to find, identify, or contact people within their university community
* prefers desktop apps over other types of applications
* can type fast and prefers typing to mouse interactions
* is reasonably comfortable using CLI apps
**Value proposition**: CampusContacts helps university students and teaching staff find and identify people they interact with, while being faster than using a typical mouse-driven GUI application.
Priorities: High (must have) - `* * *`, Medium (nice to have) - `* *`, Low (unlikely to have) - `*`
| Priority | As a …                | I want to …                                | So that I can…                                                 |
| `* * *`  | new user              | see usage instructions                     | refer to instructions when I forget how to use the App         |
| `* * *`  | student               | add a teaching staff member                | easily retrieve their details when I need academic help        |

(For all use cases below, the **System** is `CampusContacts` and the **Actor** is the `user`, unless specified otherwise)
1.  User requests to add a contact by providing their name, role, email, phone number, and location.
2.  System adds the contact and displays a success message.
* 1a1. System shows an error message indicating an argument is not in the correct format.
* 1b. User adds a contact with a name that already exists.
* 1b1. System assigns the contact an index in that name bucket and displays a suffix when needed to distinguish it.
1.  User requests to delete a specific person by their exact display name, optionally including its suffix.
2.  System deletes the person and displays a success message.
* 1a. The provided name does not match any existing contact.
* 1a1. System shows an error message indicating no contact exists with that name.
1. User requests the full details of a contact using its display name, for example `show John Tan_2`.
2. System opens a popup containing the contact's saved details.
* 1a. The provided name and suffix do not identify any contact in the address book.
* 1a1. System shows an error message and does not open a popup.
1.  User requests to search for contacts using keywords across one or more fields (e.g. name, role, location).
2.  System searches through the stored contacts.
3.  System displays a list of all matching contacts.
* 2a. No contacts match the provided search term.
* 2a1. System displays a message indicating that no matching contacts were found.
1.  Should work on any _mainstream OS_ as long as it has Java `25` or above installed.
2.  Should be able to hold up to 1000 contacts without noticeable sluggishness in performance for typical usage.
3.  Should be able to return and display results within 2 seconds when searching through a contact list of up to 1000 contacts.
4.  Should gracefully handle identical contact names without crashing.

5.  A user with above average typing speed for regular English text (i.e. not code, not system admin commands) should be able to accomplish most of the tasks faster using commands than using the mouse.
* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS
* **Teaching staff**: Professors, lecturers, teaching assistants, or tutors who interact with students within the university
* **Location**: Represents the primary physical location for a contact, symbolizing a home address or residential hostel for students, and an office or cubicle for teaching staff
* **PersonIndex**: A zero-based identifier unique within contacts that share the same base name. It is used for storage and to derive a displayed suffix.
* **Name bucket**: The group of contacts with the same base name.

testers are expected to do more *exploratory* testing.

Use a disposable data folder and add two contacts named John Tan with distinct phone/email values.
1. Run `recent` before viewing a profile. The empty-state message should explain `show`.
1. Run `list`, `show John Tan`, close the popup, `show John Tan_2`, then close the popup and run `recent`. Order: John Tan_2, John Tan.
1. Open John Tan again, close the popup, then run `recent`. Order: John Tan, John Tan_2, with no duplicate.
1. Try `show Missing Person` and `recent extra`. They should report errors without changing history.
1. Open nine additional distinct contacts (using `list` if hidden). `recent` must show only the latest ten distinct contacts; evicted contacts remain available with `list`.
1. Run `sort name desc`, then `recent`: latest-first order should return. Run `list`: your saved name-descending order should return.
1. Exit normally and restart in the same folder. `recent` should preserve membership and order.
1. Delete a viewed contact, add a replacement reusing its suffix, and run `recent`. The replacement must not inherit history.
1. Run `clear`, then `no`: history remains. Repeat with `yes`: contacts and history remain empty after restart.
The automated `RecentWorkflowTest` additionally injects ordinary IO and permission failures during `show` saves
and verifies that neither history nor active recent-view order changes. GUI popup rendering is a separate manual check.
Use a disposable data folder. Add two contacts named John Tan with different phone/email values.
1. Run `favourite John Tan_2`, then `favourites`. Only the second John Tan should appear.
1. Repeat `favourite John Tan_2`. It should report `Already in favourites` and remain a single favourite, not a duplicate.
1. Run `sort name desc`, `list`, then `favourites`. The selected sort is retained.
1. Run `unfavourite John Tan_2`. The active favourite view should immediately become empty.
1. Repeat `unfavourite John Tan_2`. It should report `Not in favourites` and leave the view empty.
1. While the view is empty, run `favourite John Tan`. The unsuffixed contact should appear.
1. Run `favourite John Tan_0`, `favourites extra`, and `favourite Missing Person`. Each should report an error without changing selections.
1. Exit normally and relaunch in the same folder. Run `favourites`; the selection should survive.
1. Delete the favourite, add another contact with the same name, and run `favourites`. The replacement must not inherit the selection.
1. Mark a contact; run `clear`, then `no`. Its selection should remain. Repeat `clear`, then `yes`: contacts and selections should both be empty after restart.
1. Deleting a person while all persons are being shown
1. Prerequisites: List all persons using the `list` command, with multiple persons in the list.
Expected: The unsuffixed John Tan contact is deleted. The status message shows the deleted contact's details.
Expected: The contact displayed as John Tan_2 is deleted, while the unsuffixed John Tan remains.
Expected: No person is deleted. The status message shows error details.
1. Other incorrect delete commands to try: `delete`, `delete John Tan_`, `delete John Tan_0`
1. Prerequisites: Use a disposable writable folder and the same JAR in two terminal windows.
1. Launch the first instance, then try to launch the second from the same working directory.
Expected: The second displays an already-in-use error and does not open the contact list.
1. Dismiss the error. Add a contact in the first instance, exit normally, and relaunch.

CampusContacts is a desktop application for managing contacts in the university community, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI) while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). If you type quickly, CampusContacts can help you manage contacts faster than traditional GUI applications.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).

A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
- `add John Doe /role student /email johnd@example.com /phone 98765432 /location John street, block 123, #01-01` : Adds a student contact named `John Doe`.
- `show John Doe` : Opens John Doe's full contact details.
- `delete John Doe` : Deletes John Doe from the contact list.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
- Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add NAME /role ROLE /email EMAIL /phone PHONE /location LOCATION`, replace `NAME` with `John Doe` and `ROLE` with `student`.
- Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `[t/TAG]` means that a tag such as `t/friend` may be supplied or omitted.
- Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
- Prefixed fields can be in any order. For `add`, the name must come before all prefixed fields.
For example, `add John Doe /phone 98765432 /location COM1 /email johnd@example.com /role student` is also acceptable.
- Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.

- If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
Opens an in-app guide containing the available commands and examples.
Adds a person to the contact list.
Format: `add NAME /role ROLE /email EMAIL /phone PHONE /location LOCATION [/major MAJOR] [/year YEAR] [/faculty FACULTY] [/department DEPARTMENT] [/hours HOURS] [/photo FILE_PATH] [t/TAG]...`
- The name, role, email, phone number, and location are all required and must not be blank.
- Write the name first, without an `n/` prefix. The remaining fields may appear in any order.
- Separate each prefix from its value with a space, except for tags written as `t/TAG`.
- Each required prefix (`/role`, `/email`, `/phone`, and `/location`) must appear exactly once; repeated non-tag prefixes are rejected, even with identical values.
- Students may optionally use `/major` and `/year`; professors may optionally use `/faculty`, `/department`, and `/hours`. Fields belonging to the other role are rejected.
- Location is stored in the existing address field. It may contain spaces and punctuation.
- `/photo` is optional. Its value must be the path to a readable PNG, JPG, JPEG, or GIF file.
- CampusContacts copies the selected image into its own data folder. You may safely move or delete the original image after adding the contact.
- When different contacts use the same source image, CampusContacts saves separate copies for them.
- Tags are optional and use the `t/TAG` syntax.
If a contact already has the same name, CampusContacts assigns it a distinct display suffix. For example, adding a second `John Tan` displays it as `John Tan_2`.
**Tip:** A person can have any number of tags, including zero.
- `add John Doe /role student /email johnd@example.com /phone 98765432 /location COM1, #02-01 /major Computer Science /year 2`

Mark people you contact often so you can find them quickly.

Omitting the suffix selects the unsuffixed contact, not every contact with that name.
Marking or unmarking works across the whole address book, even if the contact is hidden by the current filter.
Marking a contact reports `Added to favourites`; unmarking it reports `Removed from favourites`.
Repeating either command leaves the contact in the same state and reports `Already in favourites`

`favourites` replaces the current filter and displays favourite contacts in your selected `sort` order.
If there are none, the feedback explains how to mark one. Unmarking a contact while viewing favourites
removes it from the list immediately. Use `list` to show all contacts again. Adding a contact also returns
to the full list. After a restart, all contacts are shown until you run `favourites` again.
Examples (after adding two contacts named John Tan):
- `favourite John Tan_2` marks only the suffixed contact.
Favourites are saved automatically with your contacts. Deleting a contact also removes it from favourites;
a new contact using the same name and suffix starts unmarked. Confirmed `clear` removes all selections;
cancelling `clear` leaves them unchanged. If you manually remove a contact from the data file,

Sorts the displayed persons by a field.
- `name` sorts by lexicographical order of names.
- `phone` sorts by numerical order of phone numbers.
- `add` sorts by most recent added person to oldest.
- `edit` sorts by most recent edited person to oldest.
- The sort direction defaults to ascending.
- Sorting changes the displayed order only and does not change the saved address-book data.
- Specifically, when using `sort name desc`, the indices following the name are also placed in reverse order.
- `sort name` sorts contacts alphabetically by name.
- `sort phone desc` sorts contacts by phone number in descending order.
- `sort name desc` applied to `[Alice, Alice_2, Bob]` displays `[Bob, Alice_2, Alice]`.
- `sort edit` effectively pushes last edited person to the top of the list.
Edits an existing person in the contact list.

Format: `edit NAME[_NUMBER] [/name NAME] [/phone PHONE] [/email EMAIL] [/location LOCATION] [/major MAJOR] [/year YEAR] [/faculty FACULTY] [/department DEPARTMENT] [/hours HOURS] [/photo FILE_PATH or [blank]] [t/TAG or /tag TAG]...`
- Edits the person with the specified `NAME`.
- Editing works across the whole address book, even if the contact is hidden by the current filter.
- At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
- Existing values will be updated to the input values.
- When editing tags, all of the person's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
- To remove all of a person's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
- Use `/photo FILE_PATH` to add or replace a contact photo. Use `/photo [blank]` to remove it.
- You cannot assign professor fields (`/faculty`, `/department`, `/hours`) to a student, nor student fields (`/major`, `/year`) to a professor.

- Renaming a contact assigns the smallest available suffix for the new name. If that name already exists, the contact is added under the next available suffix. If the new name is the same as the old one, the contact keeps its current suffix.
* `edit John Doe /phone 91234567 /email johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of John Doe.
* `edit Alice /name Betsy Crower t/` Edits Alice's name to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing tags.
* `edit John Doe /location UTown Residence` Edits the location of John Doe.
Opens a popup containing a contact's display name, contact ID, role, phone number, email, location, role-specific details, tags, added/edited timestamps, and photo when one was added.
- The optional `_NUMBER` identifies a particular contact when several contacts have the same name.
- If the suffix is omitted, CampusContacts selects the unsuffixed contact.
- Showing works across the whole address book, even if the contact is hidden by the current filter.

from history, not from the address book. If `show` cannot find the contact, history stays unchanged. If saving a successful
`show` command fails, the history update is rolled back, a warning is shown, and the contact-details popup still opens.
Running `recent`, `list` or `sort` does not count as a visit.
`recent` replaces the current filter and temporarily uses history order rather than your selected sort.
Reopening a contact while viewing `recent` immediately moves it to the front. `list` returns to all contacts
in your saved sort order; adding a contact also returns to all contacts. `sort FIELD [asc|desc]` sorts the
currently displayed matches as usual; run `recent` again to restore latest-first order.
History is saved automatically with your contacts. After a restart, run `recent` to see it again.
Deleting a contact removes it from history. A new contact using the same name and suffix starts without
a visit. Confirmed `clear` also clears history; cancelling it does not. Older data files start with
empty history. If you manually edit `recentContacts` in the data file, stale references and repeats are
discarded and only the first ten distinct existing identifiers are retained.

Finds contacts whose details match the specified keywords (case-insensitive substring match).

Format: `find [/name NAME] [/role ROLE] [/phone PHONE] [/email EMAIL] [/location LOCATION] [/major MAJOR] [/year YEAR] [/faculty FACULTY] [/department DEPARTMENT] [/hours HOURS] [t/TAG or /tag TAG]...`
* Substring matching is supported (e.g. `COM` matches `COM1`, `ali` matches `Alice`, `@u.nus` matches email).
* If multiple different fields are specified, only contacts matching **all** criteria will be returned.
* If multiple keywords are given for the same field, contacts matching **any** of the keywords will be returned.
* You can search by name directly without prefix (e.g. `find Alice Bob`) or with `/name Alice`.
* `find John` returns all contacts whose names contain `john`.
* `find /location COM1` returns all contacts located in COM1.
* `find /phone 9876 /email u.nus.edu` returns contacts matching both phone and email domain.
* `find /role student /major Computer Science` returns all student contacts majoring in Computer Science.
Deletes the specified person from the contact list.
- Deletes the person with the specified `NAME`.
- The optional number identifies a particular contact with the specified name.
- The number **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
- If the number is omitted, it defaults to 1.
- Deleting works across the whole address book, even if the contact is hidden by the current filter.
- `delete Alice_2` deletes the contact displayed as `Alice_2`.
- Either `delete Betsy` or `delete Betsy_1` deletes the unsuffixed `Betsy`.
- `delete Alice_3` fails because no contact with that displayed identifier exists.
Clears all entries from the contact list.
After entering `clear`, type `yes` to confirm deletion or `no` to cancel.
If the application could not save previous changes, it will warn you before exiting. Type `yes`
to close the application anyway. Any other response cancels the exit. The window's top-right close button follows
CampusContacts automatically saves data after every command. You do not need to save manually.
The app stores its data under the working directory (the folder from which you launch the JAR): contacts are saved in
`data/campuscontacts.json`, and photos are stored in `data/photos`. Do not rename or delete files in the photos folder
while their contacts still exist; otherwise their details popup will show that the photo is unavailable.
Only one instance of CampusContacts may use a data folder at a time. If another instance is already using it,
the second launch displays an error; close the other instance before trying again. Separate home folders can be
used independently. Do not delete or rename `data/campuscontacts.json.lock` while the application is running.
It is normal for this file to remain after exit; it does not stop the next launch.
CampusContacts data is saved automatically as a JSON file at `data/campuscontacts.json` under the working directory
from which you launch the JAR. Advanced users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.
Close all instances of CampusContacts (including older versions) before editing or copying the data file.
The startup lock cannot prevent external editors or older versions from changing the file.

If your changes make the data file invalid, CampusContacts starts with an empty contact list at the next run and preserves a timestamped copy in `data/backups`. The invalid original remains on disk until you run a command (CampusContacts saves after every command). Still, we recommend backing up the file before editing it.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause the CampusContacts to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Install the app on the other computer, then copy both `data/campuscontacts.json` and the `data/photos` folder from your previous CampusContacts home folder.

CampusContacts is a desktop application for university students and staff to manage contacts in their campus community. It is based on AddressBook-Level3 (AB3), and uses Java and JavaFX. Users interact with it through commands and a graphical interface.
Given below are my contributions to the project.
* Replaced the original unique-person list with a name-bucket structure that allows multiple contacts to share the same name while assigning each contact a stable identifier.
* Added allocation and reuse of the smallest available suffix. For example, if `John Tan` and `John Tan_3` exist, a new John Tan receives `John Tan_2`.
* Kept the existing observable person list for the UI while using the buckets as the model's source of identity and storage.
* Added nested JSON storage for contacts grouped by name and suffix, so identifiers remain associated with the correct contact after restarting the app.
* Added conversion between JSON buckets and the in-memory model, including validation of suffixes and name-to-bucket consistency.
* Preserved compatibility with older flat contact data so existing data can still be loaded and migrated.
* Added tests for bucket loading, saving, invalid data, and duplicate contacts.
* Added the `show NAME[_NUMBER]` command to open a popup with a selected contact's full details.
* Used the optional suffix to distinguish contacts with the same name, while keeping the command read-only.
* Added a JavaFX details window and command tests for selection and parsing.
* Added an optional `/photo FILE_PATH` field when adding a contact.

* Validated the supplied path and image content, then copied the image into app-managed photo storage. The contact stores a reference to the managed photo rather than depending on the original file location.
* Displayed a contact's photo in the details popup and added photo cleanup when contacts are removed or an add operation fails.
* Added regression tests for photo parsing, persistence, copying, deletion, and invalid photo files.
* Replaced the external help link with an in-app command guide.
* Organized the commands into numbered sections and explained optional fields and photo input so users can learn the command format without leaving the application.
* Investigated and fixed issues involving same-name contact identifiers, contact editing, photo validation, and storage cleanup.
* Ran targeted Gradle tests and Checkstyle checks during implementation, and smoke-tested the packaged JAR by launching the application and exercising its commands.
* As team lead, coordinated feature work and integration with the team's upstream repository, including resolving merge conflicts and checking CI failures.
* Prepared release artifacts with Gradle's `shadowJar` task, checked that the JAR launched, and published release notes and the downloadable JAR on GitHub.
* Updated user-facing command documentation for contact identifiers, photo attachments, and the available commands.
* Contributed a PlantUML class diagram for the photo-storage design to the Developer Guide.
